title: Seconds ring together: in the B C# D E F# runs, each new note is a two-note cluster with the note before it
detail: Every note is now at its written pitch, but the harp keeps the last four notes ringing (the piece's cap, strings: 8 in tools/melodies/mountain-king.json, passed as listen.cap). Theme notes have T60 of 2.3 to 2.8 s, and a string is stolen only four notes later. In the stepwise runs (bars 1 and 3 of every statement), the note a semitone or whole tone below is still almost as loud as the new note for the whole of the new note. C#4 against D4 beats at 16.5 Hz; B3 and C4, C4 and C#4, and E4 and E#4 beat at 15 to 20 Hz. That roughness is heard as sour or out of tune, which is the user's complaint, even though no single string is out of tune. It gets worse as the piece speeds up, because each note has less time to decay before the next one: the worst cases are in statement 3. Grieg's theme is staccato and pizzicato, and a harpist would damp these strings.
evidence: Least-squares fit of every ringing pitch, using the exact frequencies from the engine's cue log, over each note's own span (onset + 10 ms to the next onset). On desktop, 19 of 90 notes have a 2nd (1 or 2 semitones) ringing at -6 dB or louder against the new note, and 35 of 90 at -12 dB or louder. The phone emulation run is the same: 19 and 32. Worst cases: D4 over C#4 at -1.0 dB (statement 3, t = 15.29 s), -1.8 and -2.1 dB; C#4 over B3 at -2.9 to -3.8 dB (all 3 statements); E4 over D4 at -4.1 to -6.0 dB; F#4 over E4 at -4.1 to -5.9 dB. The engine reported 168 to 170 steals, all of them four notes late. Data: notes/sea-song/r2/review-pitch/levels-desktop.json and levels-phone.json (worstSecond per note); recording: review-pitch/mountain-king-desktop.m4a.
fix: In a piece's theme, damp the previous melody note when the next one is plucked: one note plus its octave string ringing (cap 2), with a 30 to 60 ms fade. Alternatively, damp any ringing string within 2 semitones of the new note, as a harpist's étouffé. Keep cap 8 for the coda's chords only. This needs a per-section cap in the score, e.g. strings: {theme: 2, coda: 8}. Acceptance: the loudest ringing 2nd is -20 dB or quieter 50 ms after each onset, re-measured with the same fit.

title: The soft octave string's level is random from note to note: it lands on the main string's 2nd partial with a random phase
detail: pieceNote adds a string at exactly 2f. pluck() now makes the main string's 2nd partial 2f·1.00015 (+0.26 cents, 0.06 to 0.13 Hz away), and every partial gets a random start phase (ph: R()). The two components therefore add with a frozen random phase. The combined octave can be anything from about -2.5 dB to near cancellation against the fundamental, instead of a steady soft doubling. Round 1's detunes turned this into beating; round 2 turns it into chance. As a result, brightness jumps from note to note, and the 'soft octave for small speakers' is missing on some notes. The same thing makes the final chord's top B4 swell and fade: three near-unison components (B4's string at 493.69 Hz, B3's octave string at 493.80 Hz and B3's 2nd partial at 493.88 Hz) drift slowly in and out of phase. On a phone speaker, where the fundamentals of B3 to E4 are mostly lost, a cancelled octave leaves the 3rd partial in front (F#5 on a B3), so which pitch leads changes between notes.
evidence: 48 theme notes have no note of the same pitch class in the four before, so each octave measured belongs to one note. Their octave-above level against the fundamental runs from -20.4 to -2.7 dB on desktop (median -4.9) and from -22.8 to -2.6 dB in the phone run. The same note differs between runs: A4 (index 73) is -22.8 dB in the phone run. The independent expectation is about -5 dB. Final chord ring-out: the B4 band has 31 dB of slow amplitude modulation, D5 30 dB, F#5 29 dB. Phone-speaker model (a 4th-order high-pass at 700 Hz applied to the measured levels): the octave leads on 54 of 78 theme notes and the 3rd partial (a twelfth above) on 24, including the opening B3, where F#5 leads by 13.5 dB. The model is not a measured phone, so check it on the user's Android phone.
fix: Give harp strings a fixed start phase for all partials (ph 0, or one phase per note). A real pluck has a defined phase. With that, coincident components add predictably. Better still for a piece, drop the extra string and raise the main string's 2nd partial by the dbl amount, so there is one string per note and no near-unisons. Then set the octave level, e.g. -6 dB steady. Acceptance: octave level within ±1.5 dB across all notes and runs, and no more than 3 dB of slow AM in the final chord's ring-out.

title: Pointer harp: the D accent string now coincides exactly with the D4 copy, and the pair can cancel
detail: harpNote still adds the turn's accent, string(base*4, 0.5*amp). It is now exactly D4 with the note's shared detune, the same frequency as the Gaussian D4 copy. Round 1 used 293.66 Hz with its own random detune. The two strings add with random phase, so the low D (the winding-count note of palette B, which the user approved) is loud on one crossing and almost gone on the next. The other copies coincide with the 2nd partials of the copy below them in the same way, so each crossing's octave balance is random. Round 1 had the same pairs beating at about 1 Hz instead.
evidence: Recording of Hear the function on F(z) = z, Phase view, two counter-clockwise loops round the zero at |z| = 0.58 (review-pitch/pointer-harp-loop.m4a, cue log cues-pointer.json). D4 against D5: -1.1 dB on the first D and -20.4 dB on the second; the independent expectation is -3.0 and -4.3 dB. E5 against E4/E5: -14.9 dB and -1.8 dB on the two loops; B5: -8.1 dB and -14.5 dB. The pitches themselves are in tune; see pitch-6.
fix: Add the accent's amplitude to the D4 copy (one string), or give the accent a fixed phase relation to it. The fixed-phase pluck from pitch-2 also fixes the coincident copies. Acceptance: D4 level on repeated identical D crossings within ±1.5 dB, and the D4 accent at least +2 dB against the other notes' corresponding copy, as palette B specifies.

title: Repeated notes and octaves that ring together have independent detunes, so they swell slowly
detail: Each pieceNote draws its own ±1.5-cent detune. When the same pitch is played again within the four-note ring (F# D F#, E# C# E#, and so on), or B3 and B4 overlap in the coda, the old and new strings differ by up to 2.6 cents. That is a 0.5 to 0.7 Hz slow swell, which is hard to hear as a beat but adds chorus. A real harp re-plucks the same string.
evidence: Cue log, desktop: 24 same-pitch re-strikes within four notes, with detune differences of -2.34 to +2.60 cents (F#4 re-struck 0.34 s later, 2.6 cents apart, gives 0.56 Hz). Coda: chord 2's B4 against B3's octave string is 2.5 cents apart (0.7 Hz).
fix: Use one detune per pitch class for the whole piece, or none. Or damp the old string on a re-strike, which the pitch-1 fix does.

title: The final B-minor chord beats about 1 Hz on its fifth (equal temperament plus independent detunes)
detail: In the last chord's ring-out, B3's 3rd partial (741.0 Hz) sits about 1 Hz from F#4's 2nd partial and its octave string (740.0 and 739.9 Hz). This is the normal beating of an equal-tempered fifth, slightly changed by the per-note detunes. It is the only remaining true beat in the piece, and it falls on the last sound.
evidence: Partial frequencies of the final chord from the cue log: 741.00, 740.02 and 739.91 Hz. F#5 band in the ring-out: slow amplitude modulation, partly mixed with the random-phase effect in pitch-2.
fix: Optional: give the coda's chord notes one shared detune and tune F#4 as a just fifth over B3 (+2 cents), which costs nothing audible elsewhere. Or leave it, since every equal-tempered instrument does this.

title: Pitch, octave, timing, dynamics and ending are right. Desktop and phone emulation measure the same.
detail: The example was recorded as the app plays it, through the curve menu's Listen along, both on desktop at 1440 × 900 and in Android Chrome emulation (412 × 915, touch, long-press menu, Android UA). Both used the worklet engine at 48 kHz, with late 0 and gaps 0. The cue log captured every scheduled sound with its partial frequencies.
evidence: Pitch: all 90 written notes are scheduled within ±1.5 cents of the written pitch. Measured in the audio, they are -2.6 to +2.4 cents on desktop (SD 1.1, window bias from neighbours) and -2.1 to +2.3 on phone, and within 1.53 / 1.83 cents of the scheduled frequency. The written octave is the strongest component on 89 of 90 notes. The exception is a repeated F#4, where the previous F#'s octave string adds. Nothing sounds an octave below except chord notes. Octave strings are exactly 2.000. Main-string partials are +0.26, +0.69, +1.30 and +2.07 cents. Notes are exactly Grieg's: B C# D E F# D F# | E# C# E# E C E | B C# D E F# D F# B | A F# D F# A, three times, then the B-minor rolls. Unwritten notes: none. There are 184 cues = 90 × 2 strings + 4 drum ticks. A spectral-flux detector found all 94 cue times; its 26 extra peaks are ripples inside ringing notes, with no new spectral peak. Timing: onsets at most 9.9 ms from the score (SD 1.7 ms); successive gaps within 3.1 % (6.4 ms), below what the ear notices; quarter/eighth 1.97. The accelerando is continuous: eighths 292 → 239 ms (statement 1), 231 → 184 (2), 177 → 145 (3). Crescendo: RMS -41.4, -37.9, -34.2 dBFS by statement; the three crashes are -32.8, -32.9 and -32.9 dBFS (0.4 s) against -35.5 for statement 3's last A4, so the end is the loudest; peak -21.1 dBFS. Ending: the last chord rings out smoothly at -27 dB/s to -95 dBFS at 25.3 s, with no cut. Drum: the cut cue at F#6 (1481.5 to 1483.7 Hz, +1.7 to +4.3 cents, the old pluck as approved). It is the dominant of B minor and lands within 6 ms of each downbeat. Pointer harp: D E F# A B at -1.05 to +1.37 cents; copies exactly 1200.000 cents apart; partials as above. The diff against round 1 shows the timbre recipe unchanged (amplitudes, T60, dark filter, Gaussian, sign fifth); only the tune flag and the shared detune changed, so it is still palette B's harp, minus the chorus.
fix: None needed. Recognizable: every pitch and rhythm of Grieg's bars 1 to 4 is there. The sourness that remains comes from overlap (pitch-1) and random phases (pitch-2, pitch-3), not from wrong pitches.
